lines: Two entirely separate companies end up suffering the exact same stale data incident.
The first company's own post mortem names and disciplines the engineer who happened to push the bad configuration, and that same mistake quietly recurs months later from somebody else entirely.
The second company's own post mortem names the contributing factors instead, and the actual gap sitting inside their deploy process gets closed, permanently, for good.
So why did one company's own fix genuinely hold, while the other company's fix simply didn't.
What was actually different between them.
answer: Naming one person as the cause closes the whole investigation right at don't do that again.

Naming the contributing factors instead closes it at a far more useful place. The process itself let that happen. And that happens to be the only version of an answer that genuinely prevents a repeat.

lines: Here's a real, carefully timestamped timeline for the shop's own simulated incident.
The medium tier's own dashboard quietly goes stale for roughly an hour.
Every single stage gets its own timestamp here, running from the very first detection all the way through to full resolution.
Not a server's own CPU number, and not some abstract error rate either.
A genuine count of stale rows, and a named list of actual plant decisions that got made using them.
Those happen to be the only terms the plant operations stakeholder from the very first topic can actually judge this incident by.
A person who genuinely expects to be blamed for something will not readily tell you what actually happened.
Looking for the conditions that let an incident happen in the first place, rather than hunting for the one person who happened to trigger it, is what actually gets the honest version onto the record.
Every single contributing factor gets its own specific action item here, with a specific owner and an actual date attached.
Never some vague promise about simply being more careful going forward.
That difference is genuinely what separates a post mortem that changes something real from one that just quietly gets filed away.
Whatever gets told to the stakeholder while an incident is still actively live turns out to be a genuinely different document from the post mortem written afterward.
What's currently broken, what's actually being done about it, when to expect the next update.
This course's own later material on incident command covers exactly how that live channel actually gets staffed and run.
Pulling this together now.

A carefully timestamped timeline, impact measured in genuine data terms, contributing factors used instead of blame, action items that are actually owned, and a live update that is never the same document as the post mortem itself.
None of those four pieces is actually optional.
A post mortem names exactly one contributing factor here. The on call engineer deployed a bad configuration.
And it closes with exactly one action item. Simply retrain the engineer.
So what's genuinely missing from this entire write up.
answer: A contributing factors list of exactly one, naming a single person's own action as the cause, paired with an action item that blames rather than actually fixes anything.
The real question here, what actually let a bad configuration reach production completely undetected, never even gets asked. So that same gap stays wide open for whoever comes next.
